hints: Start from what any ligand does, then think what poly and dentate add to the meaning in terms of number of bonding sites.
Recall what type of bond a ligand always forms to a metal and what particle the ligand must supply for each bond.
walkthrough:
Remember what every ligand does**
Think of a ligand as a Lewis base sitting next to a metal ion which is electron deficient. The ligand always uses a lone pair of electrons to form a dative bond, where both electrons in the bond come from the ligand.

Add the meaning of polydentate**
Mono means one, bi means two, poly means many. Dentate refers to teeth biting onto the metal. So a polydentate ligand has several donor atoms in the same species, each supplying a lone pair, so one ligand forms several dative bonds to the same metal ion. EDTA is hexadentate because it can form six such bonds.
Final answer: A species that donates more than one lone pair to form more than one dative / coordinate bond to a central metal atom / metal ion.

hints: Look for atoms in EDTA4- that possess an available lone pair, the two N atoms and the negatively charged O atoms of the four carboxylate groups.
walkthrough:
Spot the possible donors**
You need six bonds, so you need six donor atoms. In the structure, the two central $\text{N}$ atoms each have a lone pair. Each $\text{COO}^-$ group has one $\text{O}^-$ with lone pairs available for donation, while the $\text{C=O}$ oxygen is not the donor.

Circle the correct six**
Circle both $\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{N}$ nitrogens plus the four $\text{O}^-$ oxygens, one from each carboxylate arm. That gives $2 + 4 = 6$ donor atoms, matching the replacement of six water molecules in equilibrium 1.
Final answer: Circle the two N atoms and the four $\text{O}^-$ atoms (the singly bonded O in each $\text{COO}^-$ group).

hints: Write the equilibrium law for equilibrium 1, remembering which species are in solution and which pure liquid is omitted.
Work out units by putting concentration units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into your expression and cancelling.
walkthrough:
Write products over reactants**
For $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + \text{EDTA}^{4-} \rightleftharpoons \text{[CdEDTA]}^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, the stability constant has the same form as $K_c$. So $$K_{\text{stab1}} = \frac{[[\text{CdEDTA}]^{2-}]}{[[\text{Cd}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}][\text{EDTA}^{4-}]}$$ Water is omitted because it is a pure liquid with effectively constant concentration.

Deduce the units**
Put in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for each concentration: $$\text{units} = \frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})} = \frac{1}{\text{mol dm}^{-3}} = \text{mol}^{-1} \text{dm}^3$$ One concentration on top and two below leaves $1$ over concentration.

hints: Notice equilibrium 4 is equilibrium 3 minus equilibrium 2, so think how dividing their $K$ expressions cancels the common $[\text{Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ term.
walkthrough:
See equilibrium 4 as a subtraction**
Equilibrium 2 forms the methylamine complex from the aqua ion. Equilibrium 3 forms the en complex from the same aqua ion. Equilibrium 4 converts the methylamine complex directly into the en complex. So equilibrium 4 = equilibrium 3 minus equilibrium 2.

Divide the constants**
When you subtract equilibria, you divide their $K$ values. Writing out the full concentration expressions shows the $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ cancels, leaving $$K_{\text{eq4}} = \frac{K_{\text{stab3}}}{K_{\text{stab2}}}$$

hints: Recall the link between $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and check that $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{J}$ while $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{kJ}$.
Substitute $T = 298 \text{ K}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = +0.840 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +80.9 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ with consistent units.
walkthrough:
Set up the Gibbs equation with matching units**
Use $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$ Convert entropy to $\text{kJ}$: $80.9 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} = 0.0809 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$. Then $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0.840 - (298 \times 0.0809)$$

Calculate and give sign and units**
$298 \times 0.0809 = 24.1082$. So $0.840 - 24.1082 = -23.2682$. To three significant figures, $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -23.3 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the ligand exchange in equilibrium 4 is feasible at $298 \text{ K}$, driven by entropy.
Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus} = 0.840 - 298(0.0809) = -23.3 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Look at $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ with $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +80.9 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ and ask what happens to the subtracted $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ term as $T$ rises.
walkthrough:
Track the $T\Delta S$ term**
In $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is almost constant but the $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ part grows directly with $T$. Because $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is positive, a larger $T$ makes $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ larger and positive, so subtracting a larger number makes $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ more negative and the reaction more feasible.
Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative as temperature increases because $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ increases and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is positive.
